name: Freya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer customer calls about returned orders. I finished secondary school and am still new enough that I have to slow down when a return and a refund show on separate screens. I earn the usual agent wage. I use the approved AI summary now and then since another agent showed me how, but I always check the return number.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Idris works in a supermarket storeroom, and our children are grown and living on their own. We have about five months of expenses saved and some other call centres nearby. I like putting a worried caller in touch with the actual parcel. I hope to stop working one day, but Idris and I have not worked out a date from real income figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AI Plateau is much like the occasional summary I already see. I would keep checking the return number against the customer’s original message.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my shifts would remain, and five months saved gives Idris and me some breathing room. I still need practice with split returns, but a small shortcut does not scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering returns calls and compare one AI summary each week with the original message during paid hours. In the first year of this small change, I’d bring any mixed-up order numbers to the quality meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the wage, alert to a wrong refund. The parcel number matters more than how neat the summary reads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did you catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday the summary put two returns from the same customer into one case. I separated the numbers before the refund went to the wrong order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change spending?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris (my partner) and I would leave our five-month reserve where it is. It is there for bills if a washing machine breaks, not for a new purchase.

say: I’d insist on checking **return numbers** against original messages before promising a refund.
I’d show **mixed-up orders** at the quality meeting.
think: I think my **paid shifts** remain in this mild picture.
I trust our **five-month reserve** to cover an ordinary repair.
do: Keep **answering returns calls** and compare one AI summary weekly with original messages.
Bring **mixed-up order numbers** to paid quality meetings in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about wages, alert to refund errors.
S0.quote: The parcel number matters more than how neat the summary reads.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** includes checking original customer messages.
She caught **two returns** wrongly merged into one case.
She retains an **existing five-month reserve** without new saving claims.

steps.text: Keep handling returns and compare one AI summary weekly with original messages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will answer straightforward return questions before it solves the messy ones. I would ask the manager for paid correction time when an AI answer puts a refund on the wrong order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can learn a proven review screen, but a junior agent might lose shifts as the easy queue shrinks. Five months saved helps us look at nearby centres, though Idris’s storeroom wage cannot replace mine indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new AI evidence view by checking twenty old returns with the quality agent on a paid shift. If my hours fall in the first year simple replies move, I’d apply for a posted paid returns-review desk after checking its written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel. I would keep my current wage until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the rota, interested in the evidence view. I want to see the record the tool used before I sign off a refund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What case would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include the return where a refund was approved but never paid. The screen should show both the approval date and the actual transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare offers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris (my partner) and I would compare the whole week of pay with the bus cost. I would keep my current wage until another role is signed.

say: I’d ask management for **paid correction time** after automated returns.
I’d show **approved-but-unpaid refunds** in the evidence screen.
think: I think I could learn a **proven review view**.
I fear **junior shifts** may shrink despite five months saved.
do: Learn **AI evidence view** through twenty old returns on paid time in 2026.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid review work** with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages and hours; move only after signing.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, interested in testing evidence.
S1.quote: I want to see the record the tool used before I sign off a refund.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** is a paid twenty-case test, beyond occasional summaries.
Her manager request is **individual**, not a group demand.
She compares **whole-week net pay** before leaving a current wage.

steps.text: Learn new AI evidence view by testing twenty old returns on paid time
Apply for posted paid review with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours; move only when signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell agents AGI by 2028 could check the return and answer the customer in one step. Robots around 2031 arrive later, so the phone job is at risk first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my junior work might end while I still need a wage. Five months saved gives us a search window, but it could run down before a new post begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask for written cut dates and examine posted paid dispatch openings at the nearby depot. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d take a dispatch post only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel, and keep my present job until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about the wage gap, but I can compare real vacancies. Five months is enough to ask questions, not enough to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the depot role includes lifting and whether a paid worker could show me the safe way. If the job is only updating a screen, thinking AI could do that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you reach the shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris (my partner) would check the late bus home with me. A better hourly rate would be useless if I could only get there for two shifts.

say: I’d ask for **written cut dates** on returns work.
I’d warn **2028 thinking AI** reaches calls before robots.
think: I think my **junior work** could end in 2028.
I know **five months saved** may run out during a search.
do: Request **written cut dates** and inspect posted dispatch openings in 2026.
Take **posted dispatch work** after call loss only on signed after-travel bill-covering whole-week wages, hours and late-bus access.
Ask a **paid depot worker** whether lifting is involved and how to do it safely.
S2.quote: Five months saved gives us a search window, but it could run down before a new post begins.
fieldNote: She knows **2028 screen risk** comes before depot robots.
The dispatch role must have **safe lifting** and reachable late buses.
A higher hourly rate may hide **fewer paid shifts**.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid depot-dispatch openings before 2028
Take dispatch only on signed after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours and reachable late bus
Ask paid depot worker about lifting and safe instruction before accepting dispatch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us time to find out which depot jobs have paid shifts. I would ask for a trial beside a worker before taking a certificate course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could learn parcel receiving if a supervisor shows me the physical check, though AI could run the record in 2031. Robots around 2034 might reach the lifting later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d take a supervised paid receiving trial only if the depot posts a paid opening and the lifting is safe. If that role requires a safety course, I’d take it only if the employer funds the fee and paid study time. In the first year after 2031, I’d move only on a signed offer with written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare and a route home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a real trial gives me something to judge. I would rather count ten actual parcels than watch a perfect training video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test physically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a damaged box against the delivery note and record who accepted it. If the load was too heavy, I would say so before anybody offered me the post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Idris check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris (my partner) would compare the depot rota with the last bus. We have some savings, but I will not spend them on taxis to prop up a weak wage.

say: I’d request a **supervised paid trial** for a posted depot opening.
I’d ask about **safe lifting** before accepting physical work.
think: I think I could learn **parcel receiving** on a real shift.
I know **2031 AI** reaches records before 2034 robots lift.
do: Try **supervised paid receiving** only for posted opening with safe lifting.
Take **required safety course** for posted paid depot role only with employer-funded fees and paid study time.
Move after 2031 only on **signed after-fare bill-covering wages**, hours and bus home.
feel: **Anxious**, with a practical trial to judge.
S3.quote: I would rather count ten actual parcels than watch a perfect training video.
fieldNote: The **paid trial** needs a posted role and safe lifting.
The **course** requires funded fees and paid study hours.
The **last bus** and after-fare wage govern any move.

steps.text: Try supervised paid receiving only for posted opening with safe lifting
Take posted paid depot role’s required safety course only with employer-funded fees and paid time
Move only on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages, hours and last-bus access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us years to look at paid hours, not a fixed date when older staff can stop. I would ask each year how many returns shifts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still need work at 68 because Idris and I have not checked what income we would have after work. Full thinking AI may take returns in 2036, and robots around 2039 follow later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid returns calls and list our actual weekly wages, bills and savings before deciding any retirement date. If I still need a wage after 2036 and my shifts fall, I’d apply for posted paid desk work after checking its written weekly wages and hours cover bills after travel. I would keep my current job until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long end, but not helpless today. A decade lets me test what is real while I am still paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which retirement figures would you check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check any retirement figure with Idris before putting it in our plan. I cannot budget with a pension amount I have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own homes. I would not assume they can cover our bills, even if they are kind enough to visit.

say: I’d ask for **yearly returns hours** as 2036 approaches.
I’d say **older staff** may still need a wage.
think: I think I may **need work at 68**.
I cannot assume **retirement income** that I have not checked.
do: Keep **paid returns calls** and compare actual wages, bills and savings.
Apply for **posted paid desk work** if wages remain needed and shifts fall; move only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly terms.
S4.quote: A decade lets me test what is real while I am still paid.
fieldNote: She makes no **pension or retirement-date assumption**.
The **five-month cushion** supports a measured job search but cannot replace lifelong income.

steps.text: Keep paid returns calls and compare actual wages, bills and savings
Apply for posted paid desk work; move only on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest. It could handle the easy returns I am still learning, and five months saved is time to search, not a permanent wage. Written notice, paid correction time and a nearby posted job with weekly pay covering our bills after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a new job includes a whole week of paid shifts. The hourly rate is a poor guide when only two days are on the rota.

headlineQuote: The hourly rate is a poor guide when only two days are on the rota.
portrait: At **58**, Freya is a junior returns agent still learning after secondary school.
She and Idris have **grown children**, usual agent pay and about five months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI summaries occasionally** but checks original return numbers.
She tests new screens and compares **whole-week wages** before accepting local work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take easy returns before she learns enough complex cases to keep her wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid correction time and posted nearby work with bill-covering net weekly pay would help.
